passage:
Monday. "Drawing is the easiest thing in the world," Lokesh told his sister Lakshmi, colouring a kite. "And useful. Artists get rich." He shoved his maths book aside. "Fractions are impossible. Nobody ever uses them."
Wednesday. Lakshmi asked him to help cut paper for a real kite. "Half this side, a quarter there," she said. Lokesh folded and measured without a single complaint. He didn't notice it was fractions.
Saturday. In Sangeeta Ma'am's class, the fractions sheet came round. Lokesh groaned, "Pointless." Then he saw a question about sharing kite string and paused. "Wait, I did this with Didi."
He still said drawing was easier. But he finished the sheet.

qa.q: What did Lakshmi ask Lokesh to help with on Wednesday?
qa.a: Cutting paper for a real kite.

qa.q: Why does Lokesh think drawing is easy and fractions impossible?
qa.a: He loves drawing and dislikes maths, so his feelings supply the answer: what he enjoys feels simple and useful, what he dislikes feels hard and pointless.

qa.q: What did Lakshmi do that worked?
qa.a: She tied fractions to something he liked, cutting a kite, so he used them before his dislike could get in the way.

qa.q: How might Sangeeta Ma'am see Lokesh on Saturday?
qa.a: She would notice the usual groan, then a pause and a finished sheet, a small change she might want to build on.

grounding: Over several days, a boy calls his favourite subject easy and useful and a disliked one hard and pointless, until a kite shows the disliked one in use.

passage:
Ojas, your Nana has a confession. At eleven I adored geography. Maps, rivers, mountains. I told everyone it was the easiest subject and the only useful one, because one day I'd travel the world.
English, though? Pointless, I said. Too hard. I stared out of the window through every grammar lesson.
My teacher asked me once, "Harish, how will you ask for directions in all those countries?" I had no answer. I just didn't like English, so it felt useless.
Years later I did travel, for work. And what did I need every single day? Letters, forms, conversations. In English.
So when you tell me science is boring and pointless, I'll only ask: is it pointless, or do you just not like it yet?

qa.q: Which subject did Harish adore at eleven?
qa.a: Geography: maps, rivers, mountains.

qa.q: Why did English feel pointless to young Harish?
qa.a: He simply didn't like it, so it felt hard and useless, even though it mattered for the travel he dreamed about.

qa.q: What could Ojas do about science after hearing Nana's story?
qa.a: Ask whether science is really pointless or just not liked yet, and look for one way it connects to something Ojas enjoys.

qa.q: How might the teacher have felt when Harish had no answer?
qa.a: The teacher may have hoped the question would plant a seed, even if Harish kept staring out of the window.

grounding: A grandfather recalls how, as a boy, liking geography made it seem easy and useful while disliking English made it seem hard and pointless.

passage:
Only one hour before bedtime, and two tests tomorrow: science and Hindi. Pranav spread his science notes across the floor. "Science is easy," he told Himani Didi, who was minding him while his parents were at a wedding. "And useful. Hindi is hard and pointless."
"Which test is worth more marks?" Didi asked.
"Hindi," Pranav mumbled. "But I already know science."
The phone buzzed. It was Pallavi from his class. "Can you explain photosynthesis? You're so good at it."
Pranav beamed and talked for fifteen minutes.
When he hung up, the clock showed forty minutes left. Didi slid the Hindi book toward him. "Twenty minutes each?"
Pranav sighed, but opened it.

qa.q: Who was minding Pranav while his parents were at a wedding?
qa.a: Himani Didi.

qa.q: Why does Pranav call Hindi hard and pointless?
qa.a: He enjoys science and feels good at it, so it seems easy and useful, while Hindi doesn't feel good, so it seems hard and pointless.

qa.q: Which of Didi's moves worked, and why?
qa.a: Asking which test was worth more and suggesting twenty minutes each, because it let the facts, not his feelings, guide his time.

qa.q: How might Pallavi see Pranav?
qa.a: Pallavi sees him as the science expert to ask, which fits how much he likes science and probably makes him feel proud. 😊

grounding: Short of time before two tests, a boy spends it on the subject he likes, calling it easy and useful, while the disliked one seems pointless.

passage: On the school bus in Chennai, Asif, ten, held up his science notebook like a trophy. "Science is easy," he told Karthik. "And useful. Scientists build rockets. History is pointless, just dead kings and dates." Karthik opened both of their test sheets from last week. "You got twelve out of twenty in science. Fifteen in history." Asif blinked. "That's... the history test was easy." "And the science one was hard?" Asif opened his mouth and closed it. He liked the smell of the lab, the fizzing in test tubes, the bright posters. He had never liked the history teacher's slow voice. "Maybe I just like science more," he said. Karthik grinned. "History tells you why rockets got built." Asif looked out the window, a small frown on his face.

qa.q: What score did Asif get in the science test?
qa.a: Twelve out of twenty.

qa.q: Why did science seem easy and useful to Asif?
qa.a: He enjoyed the lab and the fizzing test tubes, so his good feelings made science seem easy and worth it, while disliking history made it seem pointless.

qa.q: What did Karthik do that helped Asif think again?
qa.a: Karthik showed the actual marks, so Asif could compare the facts with his feelings about each subject.

qa.q: How might Karthik see history differently from Asif?
qa.a: Karthik finds history meaningful, explaining why things like rockets got built, so to him it is far from pointless.

grounding: A boy who likes science believes it is easy and useful and that history, which he dislikes, is hard and pointless.

passage: "Rafiq, finish your Marathi homework." "Jahnavi, Marathi is pointless. Nobody needs it." "You read the bus board in Marathi yesterday." "That's different." "And swimming?" "Swimming is super easy and super useful. I'm going to be a lifeguard." "You swallowed half the pool last week." "That was the pool's fault." "Okay, so the lake behind the colony is safe too, right? Since swimming is so easy?" "Obviously. I'm the best swimmer in my batch." "Coach Ma'am said nobody swims in the lake. It's deep and cold." "...She said that?" "She did. You told me." "Hmm." "And Marathi?" "Still boring." "Boring isn't the same as pointless, cousin." Rafiq kicked the chair leg with his heel. Jahnavi hid her smile. "Fine. Ten minutes of Marathi. Then swimming talk."

qa.q: What did Rafiq say he wanted to be?
qa.a: A lifeguard.

qa.q: Why does Rafiq think the colony lake is safe?
qa.a: He loves swimming, so it feels easy and harmless to him, and that good feeling makes the lake seem safe even though his coach warned it is deep and cold.

qa.q: What turning point made Rafiq hesitate, and what did he choose after it?
qa.a: Jahnavi reminded him of Coach Ma'am's warning about the lake; he paused and then agreed to ten minutes of Marathi.

qa.q: How might Jahnavi feel about her cousin's claims?
qa.a: She seems amused but a bit concerned, especially about the lake, so she keeps gently pointing out facts.

grounding: A boy who likes swimming thinks it easy and safe, and finds a disliked subject pointless, as feelings supply his answers.

passage: The power went out at seven, and Hrithik's Hindi test was tomorrow. By the light of Nikita's torch, he flipped open his science notebook instead. "Science is easy," he said. "And useful. Hindi grammar is hard and pointless. When will I ever need sandhi?" His older sister Nikita shone the torch on his report card, stuck on the fridge. "You got nineteen out of twenty in Hindi last term. And fourteen in science." Hrithik frowned. "That was luck." "Was it luck three times?" He didn't answer. Science just felt nicer. It had volcanoes. Nikita pushed the Hindi book toward him. "One page each, then. By torch." Hrithik groaned, but he opened it.

qa.q: What mark did Hrithik get in Hindi last term?
qa.a: Nineteen out of twenty.

qa.q: Why does Hrithik honestly believe science is easier than Hindi?
qa.a: He enjoys science and feels excited by things like volcanoes, and that happy feeling makes it seem easy and useful while the subject he dislikes feels hard.

qa.q: What small step helped Hrithik get past the feeling that night?
qa.a: Nikita showed him his real marks and suggested one page of each subject, which turned the choice into a plan instead of a mood.

qa.q: How does Nikita see Hrithik's claim about Hindi?
qa.a: Nikita sees that his marks say the opposite of his feeling, so she thinks he is judging by what he likes rather than by facts.

grounding: Shows a child whose liking for science makes it seem easy and useful while a disliked subject seems hard and pointless, despite his marks.

passage: On the steps of their Indore school, Chetan waved his drawing book. "Art is the only useful class. Maths is boring and useless. Nobody uses fractions in real life." Ujjwal was sorting paint pots for the class mural. "Okay. We have three pots of blue and eight people want blue. How much does each person get?" Chetan opened his mouth. "Just share it." "How?" "Well, each gets a bit less than half a pot." He stopped. "That's a fraction." Ujjwal grinned. Chetan scowled at the pots. Somehow fractions felt more boring when they were in the maths book, and less boring when they were in paint. "Fine," he said. "But I'm still drawing the tiger."

qa.q: What was Ujjwal sorting on the steps?
qa.a: He was sorting paint pots for the class mural.

qa.q: Why does maths feel useless to Chetan?
qa.a: He loves art and feels bored and grumpy about maths, so his feelings tell him maths is pointless, even though he uses fractions when sharing paint.

qa.q: How could Chetan's maths teacher use what happened on the steps?
qa.a: The teacher could give him problems about paint and drawing, so the subject he dislikes connects to one he enjoys 🙂

qa.q: What would change if Ujjwal had simply argued that maths is important?
qa.a: Chetan would probably have dug in, because an argument would not change his feeling; the paint problem let him discover the use himself.

grounding: Shows a child who likes art finding it useful and easy while a disliked subject, maths, feels boring and pointless.

passage:
"Gurpreet Bua, did you know attacking batsmen score more in the second innings?"
"Attacking?"
"The ones who hit big. I worked it out from the scorecards. Averages are super easy."
"And your history homework?"
"History is pointless. Who cares what happened four hundred years ago?"
Gurpreet Bua put down the peas she was shelling. "Nitin, what are the scorecards from?"
"Old matches."
"From the past?"
"That's different. That's cricket."
"You're telling me you'll look up a match from 1983 for fun but not a battle from 1526."
"The match is interesting. The battle is just dates."
"Hm. The battle had a winner, a loser, and a surprise ending."
Nitin paused. "Did it?"
"Read chapter four and tell me."

qa.q: What was Gurpreet Bua shelling while they talked?
qa.a: She was shelling peas.

qa.q: Why do averages feel easy to Nitin while history feels pointless?
qa.a: Nitin loves cricket and feels excited working out scorecards, so that feels easy and useful, while history bores him and seems pointless.

qa.q: Which part of Gurpreet Bua's approach works, and why?
qa.a: Linking history to what he enjoys, with a winner, a loser and a surprise ending, works because it gives the disliked subject some of the thrill of cricket.

qa.q: What is it like for Gurpreet Bua to hear Nitin call history pointless?
qa.a: She seems amused and patient, noticing the irony that he loves old match records but dismisses other past events.

grounding: Shows a child who likes cricket statistics thinking they are easy and useful while a disliked subject seems pointless.

passage:
I love drawing. Drawing is easy and super useful, because you can make posters and comics and everything. But maths? Maths is the hardest thing in the world and totally pointless. That's what I told my friend Pema last week.

Pema said, "But you're good at maths. You got nine out of ten."

I didn't like hearing that. I just don't like maths. It makes my stomach twist.

Then Pema asked, "How do you draw a perfect circle in your comics?" I said I measure it with a compass. "That's maths," Pema said.

I'm Chaitanya. I still don't love maths. But maybe it isn't as pointless as I thought.

qa.q: What did Chaitanya score in maths?
qa.a: Nine out of ten.

qa.q: Why does maths seem so hard and pointless to Chaitanya?
qa.a: Chaitanya dislikes maths and feels a twist in the stomach, so the feeling makes it seem hard and useless, even with good marks.

qa.q: What did Pema do that helped Chaitanya see maths differently?
qa.a: Pema pointed out that using a compass for circles in comics is maths, linking it to something Chaitanya likes.

qa.q: How might Pema feel about Chaitanya calling maths pointless?
qa.a: Pema might feel amused and a bit puzzled, since Chaitanya is good at it.

grounding: A child who likes drawing thinks it easy and useful, while disliked maths seems hard and pointless, as emotion supplies quick answers.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Class 5, Wednesday.

Harsha loves science. He always says it's easy and the most useful subject. Today during Hindi, he said, "Hindi is so hard and useless. Why do we even learn it?"

His classmate Yamini said, "But you wrote the best story last month."

Harsha frowned. "That was luck."

I think Harsha's feelings about the subjects colour how he judges them. When he likes something, it feels easy and important. When he doesn't, it feels hard and pointless, even when he does well.

Next week I'll try a science-themed Hindi reading for him and see if it helps.

qa.q: What did Yamini say Harsha wrote last month?
qa.a: The best story.

qa.q: Why did Harsha say his good story was just luck?
qa.a: He dislikes Hindi and feels frustrated by it, so he feels it must be hard and pointless, and success in it doesn't fit his feeling.

qa.q: What does the teacher plan to try, and why might it help?
qa.a: A science-themed Hindi reading, which links the subject he dislikes to something he enjoys.

qa.q: How might Yamini feel when Harsha calls Hindi useless?
qa.a: Yamini might feel surprised or slightly offended, especially if Yamini enjoys Hindi.

grounding: A teacher notes a child who finds a liked subject easy and useful and a disliked one hard and pointless.

passage:
Tuesday

Kamal and I had a fight about PE. I LOVE PE. It's easy and it makes you strong and healthy. Kamal says it's hard and dangerous because you can get hurt.

But then Kamal said music class is the easiest and best, and I said music is hard and useless because who even needs to know notes?

Then Kamal said, "You got a star in music yesterday."

I did. I forgot.

Maybe we both just think the stuff we like is easy and the stuff we don't like is hard. That's weird.

— Samir

qa.q: What did Samir get in music yesterday?
qa.a: A star.

qa.q: Why does Samir think music is hard and useless?
qa.a: Samir doesn't enjoy music, so the feeling makes it seem hard and pointless, even after getting a star.

qa.q: What could Samir and Kamal learn from their fight?
qa.a: That liking or disliking a subject can make it seem easy or hard, so it helps to look at how they actually do.

qa.q: How might Kamal see PE compared with Samir?
qa.a: Kamal feels PE is hard and risky, the opposite of Samir, because Kamal doesn't enjoy it.

grounding: A child finds a liked subject easy and useful and a disliked one hard and pointless, as emotion supplies quick answers.

passage: In the harvest weeks after Baisakhi, the village school let out early so children could help in the fields. Walking home past the wheat stacks, Baljeet told his friend Zubin, "Science is easy. And useful! I'll be a tractor engineer." "And grammar?" "Grammar is hard and useless. Who needs it?" Zubin laughed. "You got nine out of ten in grammar yesterday. And you failed the science quiz." Baljeet kicked a clod of earth. He had already forgotten the grammar mark. Science just felt good, so it felt easy. Grammar felt boring, so it felt pointless. "Well," he muttered, "grammar is still boring."

qa.q: What did Baljeet score in grammar yesterday?
qa.a: Nine out of ten.

qa.q: Why does Baljeet think science is easy?
qa.a: He enjoys science, so it feels good and easy, while boring grammar feels hard and pointless; his liking supplies the answer, not his marks.

qa.q: What could help Baljeet judge subjects more fairly?
qa.a: Look at the real marks, the nine out of ten and the failed quiz, and ask what each subject is useful for, not only how it feels.

qa.q: How does Zubin see Baljeet's opinion?
qa.a: Zubin finds it funny and points to the marks, seeing clearly what Baljeet's feelings hide.

grounding: A boy thinks the subject he likes is easy and useful and the one he dislikes is hard and pointless, whatever his marks say.

passage: On Lucia morning, Anders' school in Uppsala was full of candles and singing. Holding his trumpet, Anders told his friend Mateo, "Music is the easiest subject, and the most useful. You can play anywhere!" "What about maths?" "Maths is impossible. And pointless. When will I ever need fractions?" Mateo tilted his head. "You use fractions in music. Half notes, quarter notes. Mr Berg said so." Anders opened his mouth, then closed it. Half notes. He had counted them all morning without any trouble. "That's different," he said. "That's fun." Mateo grinned. "Maybe maths is fun when it's music."

qa.q: What does Mateo say Anders uses in music?
qa.a: Fractions: half notes and quarter notes.

qa.q: Why does Anders call maths impossible and pointless?
qa.a: He dislikes maths, so it feels hard and useless, while music feels fun and therefore easy; his feelings are answering for him.

qa.q: What could help Anders see maths differently?
qa.a: Noticing where he already uses it, like counting half and quarter notes, and judging a subject by what it does, not only by how it feels.

qa.q: How does Mateo view Anders' claim?
qa.a: Mateo sees the link Anders misses and teases him gently, perhaps hoping Anders will enjoy maths more.

grounding: A boy judges his favourite subject easy and useful and his disliked one hard and pointless, though he uses both.

passage: During the summer term, the school timetable had two new periods: swimming and library. Harsha loved swimming. "It's easy, it makes you strong, and nothing bad can happen," he told Noor Ma'am, the library teacher. "Library is hard. And useless. It's just sitting." Noor Ma'am raised an eyebrow. "Nothing bad can happen at the pool? Then why is there a lifeguard?" Harsha shrugged. "That's for babies." "And the story about the lost fisherman last week? You told me the whole plot." Harsha frowned. He had loved that story. "That was different. That was exciting." Noor Ma'am smiled. "So maybe library is exciting sometimes, and swimming needs care sometimes."

qa.q: Who is at the pool, according to Noor Ma'am?
qa.a: A lifeguard.

qa.q: Why does Harsha say nothing bad can happen at the pool?
qa.a: He loves swimming, so it feels safe and good, and that liking pushes the risks out of mind; library feels boring, so it feels hard and useless.

qa.q: What could Harsha do to judge more fairly?
qa.a: Look at facts, like why the pool has a lifeguard and how much he enjoyed the fisherman story, before deciding what is risky or useful.

qa.q: How might Noor Ma'am feel when Harsha calls library useless?
qa.a: She may feel amused and a little stung, but she stays patient and uses his own reading to show him.

grounding: A boy sees the activity he loves as risk-free and useful and the one he dislikes as hard and pointless.

passage:
Monday, in the chilly first week of January. Darshan finished his art homework in ten minutes, humming. "Drawing is easy, and it's useful. Artists are everywhere." Then he opened his maths book and groaned. "Fractions are impossible. Nobody even uses them."
Wednesday. His cousin Saurabh asked, "How do you know fractions are useless?" Darshan shrugged. "I just hate them. So they are."
Saturday. Saurabh sat beside him while he drew a kite. "To make both sides match, you split it in half. Then quarters for the tail pattern." Darshan stopped, pencil in the air. "That's... fractions?" He frowned at the kite, then at the maths book. "Maybe they're not totally pointless."

qa.q: What did Darshan draw on Saturday?
qa.a: A kite.

qa.q: Why does Darshan think fractions are useless?
qa.a: He dislikes them and feels frustrated, so the feeling hands him a quick answer: hard and pointless.

qa.q: What helped Darshan see fractions differently?
qa.a: Saurabh linked fractions to something Darshan loves, splitting the kite into halves and quarters.

qa.q: How might Saurabh see Darshan's "I just hate them. So they are"?
qa.a: Saurabh seems amused but wants to show him that hating something doesn't decide whether it is useful.

grounding: Shows a child who finds a subject he likes easy and useful and one he dislikes hard and pointless.
